Rev: Bronson owes a little or a lot to Kubrick s Clockwork Orange, but if that s a crime I wish more people would commit it.
Bronson invites you to admire its protagonist as a pure, muscular embodiment of anarchy. And perhaps you will, but you may also be glad that he s still behind bars.

Whether it s Peterson/Bronson s more theatrical bits or his untamable character s many blood-spitting, knuckle-beating, explosions, Hardy chomps down on his once-in-a-career role with stunning ferocity and never lets go. He s extraordinary.

There are two Bronsons on display here: the impossible thug that we don t dare release into polite society, and the guy we enjoy watching do his terrible thing. The man and the movie are both living, punching contradictions.
Refn has somehow found his way to an authentic English hard-man drama, anchored in a dynamite performance, even as it celebrates thug life.
He s neither victim nor hero, but a man who, in every conceivable sense, belongs behind bars.
This is unhinged genius, an amazing piece of acting. Brutal, yes, but magnetic all the same.
Refn s artful and energetic film never goes further than face value.
This movie and Hardy s electrifying performance will knock you for a loop.
Tom Hardy gives an amazing performance as Peterson, who took on the nickname Charlie Bronson, after the Death Wish actor.
The tone is surreal, at once visceral and clinical, making Bronson an unsettling experience: savage, disturbing, and yet somehow fascinating.
It is 92 minutes of rage, acted by Tom Hardy.
Hardy is remarkable, however. This is an actor with a memorably expressive rasp of a voice, both blunt and musical.
Bronson isn t a story in the traditional sense at all. It s a meditation on the art of rage - an action painting passing itself off as an action movie.
It s played with real zest and energy, and if you can stand the heat it gives off it may charm you despite yourself.
With an intelligent, provocative and stylized approach, Bronson (based on a true story) follows the metamorphosis of Mickey Peterson into Britain s most dangerous prisoner, Charles Bronson.
It s lively and vivid but ends up leaving the viewer indifferent to the central character, his life, and his dubious place in British pop culture.
Too smart/arty for the slasher set, and too violent for high-brows, Bronson may have a tough time finding its niche, although it has cult hit written all over it.
Bronson is one of those based on a true story dramatizations where the theatrically staged drama only gets in the way of the more interesting truth.
Despite the artistic flourishes, this is still an utterly repellent look at a psychopath who does not deserve the attention of the filmmakers or the audience.
Bronson is essentially a faux-operatic, music hall turn--a larky, lumpen version of Lola Mont s.
It s an assaultive work about an assaultive fellow.
This is such a rare movie. Its characters are uncompromisingly themselves, flawed, stubborn, vulnerable.
Mr. Malkovich is one of the few actors capable of conveying genuine intellectual depth.
As fiercely unsentimental as Disgrace is, it offers by the end a measure of hope, and because that hope is so hard-won, it has the ring of truth.
The austere economy of Coetzee s writing, crisply adapted for the screen by Anna Maria Monticelli, plays out the melodrama with quietly brooding menace.
John Malkovich has played some odd ducks in his career, but for sheer unsavoriness, few can match the blandly monstrous Cape Town poetry professor he brings to off-putting life in Disgrace.
Surprisingly successful adaptation of J. M. Coetzee s superb novel.
I cannot tell a lie. I derive great satisfaction watching John Malkovich act.
Newcomer Jessica Haines is transparent and heartbreaking as the prof s unorthodox daughter, a victim of violence as the old ways crumble.
It s a harsh experience, at times engrossing, at other times stiff and unconvincing, but it asks a necessary question: What happens to the country s whites after white rule is gone?

Anchored by another marvelously quirky yet deadly serious performance from John Malkovich, and likely to be relished by the fan base of J.M. Coetzee s Booker Prize-winning novel, this is a strong, perceptive, old-school arthouse picture.

The movie eventually begins to wilt under the sober, plodding direction of Steve Jacobs, but the thoughtful screenplay gives Malkovich a complex, increasingly reflective character arc that he plays with great feeling, making the professor s redemption seem honestly won.
Nothing is simple in this film, which ramifies into parallel meditations on race, the transformation of racial politics and lessons to be learned from the lives of dogs.
Absorbing but often bloodless and, frankly, depressing.
After a compelling opening act and some shocking late-film developments, the film feels disengaged from the action at hand and the issues raised.
The story often appears a little unreal.
Is it a great movie? John Malkovich s portrayal of an aging and sexually aggressive professor of poetry is enough to make the film worth anyone s while.
A frustrating film full of overplayed men-as-dogs metaphors, it s only watchable for Malkovich, who could probably read a social studies exam and still be commanding.
The film, unfortunately, hasn t the depth Malkovich brings to his performance.

It s a modest film, if only in scale and apparent budget, about some of the greatest questions in life, like the existence of God, our capacity to see beyond our own vanity and the legacies of fathers, both blood and state.
At its core, A Screaming Man emphasizes the strength of family bonds. It s a sad, moving portrait that has nothing to do with its chaotic setting.
Haroun s tender but unsentimental regard for his characters allows his storytelling a natural gravitas thoroughly suited to the simultaneously unfolding private and national tragedies.

A collective sense of psychological turmoil seems to weigh heavily on the entire country as much as Champ, reaching critical mass once chaos creeps into the city-leading to a quiet, climactic walk into darkness that earns the right to be called haunting.
Haroun is uninterested in big war scenes and is best at evoking the little details of life.

The first half-hour is as evocative as (and more specific than) Claire Denis White Material, a similarly broad treatment of post-colonial chaos. The rest, sadly, falls apart, but Haroun s formal skill confirms his continual promise.
Haroun is achingly conscious of day-to-day decisions that seem small when they re made but can suddenly loom large.
The characterizations never comfortably accommodate Haroun s pat metaphor, though his stoic visual storytelling has an oblique gravity.
Never indulging in outright scare tactics or loose improvisation, the movie primarily works like an awkward narrative that plays with perspective.
Smartly written and flawlessly acted, Lovers of Hate is a Trojan horse, the kind of movie that begins so self-effacingly that we don t expect any surprises.
If you were ever wondering what Die Hard would have been like if Neil LaBute directed it as an art film, prepare to enjoy Lovers of Hate.
Lovers of Hate would be a family tragedy if the immature antics of the three characters didn t send you ping-ponging from sympathetic chuckles to guffaws of disgust.
A 2010 Sundance favorite, this inventive (and inventively thrifty) character study from Austin indie stalwart Bryan Poyser never flinches from the intractable sibling resentment at its core.
It s a movie that doesn t inspire anything as passionate as love or hate.
The movie is witty only on occasion. But it lingers in the mind, thanks largely to its trio of actors -- especially Alex Karpovsky.
Designed to make you laugh and squirm, Lovers of Hate does more of the latter.
At once an unsentimental portrait of the ambitious singer who thought himself bound for glory, and an affecting elegy for a time when song was a form of revolution.

Many of the interviews in the film conducted with everyone from family members to Christopher Hitchens and Tom Hayden look to be 10, even 20, years old. Together they concoct a complex portrait of an ultimately unknowable man.
Beautiful and melodic as well as pointedly political.

Briskly constructed and rich in Ochs music and period notables, Kenneth Bowser s film will be a must for the artist s fans, but its fresh take on an overexamined decade should also appeal to Kennedy-era completists.
Kenneth Bowser s terrific documentary is a poignant portrait of an uncompromising artist.
The story told by Mr. Bowser s film is complicated and tragic.
Though hewing to a too-conventional structure, Bowser s film is densely researched enough to yield insights not just into its overlooked subject, but also into his overly analyzed era.
Though Bowser uses old footage when possible, the absence of his subject -- who died tragically in 1976 -- is keenly felt.

It s a well-constructed and long-overdue tribute, yet Fortune refrains from delving into larger questions that surround Ochs s work. Did the singer s unwavering dedication to agitpop leave him stranded in the 60s? And does Ochs s diminished legacy among today s essentially apolitical neofolkies amount to a second tragedy?
Not only is a good look at a man who carved a small but important niche into the folk world but a good record of the turbulent 1960s and what motivated its protesters.
A slick, exciting, well-made crime thriller, dripping with atmosphere.

Digitally shot, the film looks great, and the performances ooze charisma. The biggest star, though, may be Kinshasa itself, a roiling, barely cohesive sea of humanity that seems as if it could serve as a backdrop for some fascinating films for years to come.
As gut-punch storytelling, Viva Riva! delivers much, not the least of which is the promise of an exciting new filmmaking talent.
The first major motion picture to come out of Congo in decades happens to be one of the best neonoirs from anywhere in recent memory.

Driven by its charismatic upstart gangster protagonist Riva, the film is one joyride that knows it will careen into a spectacular crash. Djo Tunda wa Munga captures the particular vibe released by this mixture of carpe diem and self-destructive instinct.

Martin Scorsese, meet Djo Tunda Wa Munga, because you obviously have a lot in common. Viva Riva! is nothing less than the Congolese Mean Streets, oozing sexual heat and brute violence and powered by a locomotive s worth of raw kinetic energy.

Frenetic, sleazy, and entertaining as all hell, Viva Riva! is a stylish and (save for the NC-17 it d certainly earn) multiplex-worthy crime drama from, of all unexpected places, the Democratic Republic Of The Congo.
Directed by Djo Tunda Wa Munga, who studied filmmaking in Belgium, this is raw, sardonic, and formally complex.

Repackaging the revenge thriller in parakeet colors and distinctive African beats, the Congolese writer and director Djo Tunda Wa Munga gives Viva Riva! a playful sensuality that goes a long way toward disguising formula.
Writer-director Djo Tunda Wa Munga deplores the corruption, gunplay, and oversexed misogyny plaguing his country - and he s going to show you as much of it as possible before the end credits roll.
On the basis of this expertly engineered crime thriller Djo Munga is a director going places.
It takes from American gangster classics (White Heat and both Scarface films come to mind) but its unique setting and underlying themes give it distinction.

A fast-moving Congolese crime thriller loaded with graphic sex and violence - basically an exploitation picture. But it s hard to surrender to the gritty flow because the story is stitched together from such crushingly familiar bits.
The first from the Democratic Republic of Congo to be distributed in the U.S. That in itself is worthy of some kind of celebration, even if Viva Riva! too lazily indulges in shapeless genre excess.
Unfortunately, despite the sweaty, tense atmosphere, Viva Riva becomes derivative of the duller scenes in other gangster flicks.
The near-slapstick escapes sit uneasily with the raw bits of very adult sex and cringe-worthy close-ups of brutality that dominate the rest of the proceedings.
Thanks to Banderas and his Corinthian leather purr and writers who know how to use it, Puss is the best animated film of 2011.
It s always a pleasure to find a family film that respects its audience all the way up the line.

A treat to experience visually (especially in lively 3-D) and verbally, Puss in Boots is a family film where the adventure and invention never flag and the tongue-in-cheek humor doesn t linger far behind.

A perfectly diverting romp that happens to showcase some of the best 3D work yet from a mainstream animated feature. Colorful, clever enough, free of cloying showbiz in-jokes, action-packed without being ridiculous about it and even well choreographed.
The results are so funny and irresistible audiences are bound to be swept away into this kitty s universe.
Puss in Boots is essentially non-stop dazzling action scenes loosely connected by a thin, predictable story of greed versus good.
For a kids movie, the humor, at times, strays a bit too far into grown-up territory.
The story has just the right blend of child-centered silliness and winking adult humor.
Even if they don t provide much lift, these boots were made for amusement.
Puss in Boots isn t particularly deep, nor does it take itself seriously -- it just wants to seek glory, win affection and cash in. Done, done and done.

The movie has a devilish wit that works for parent and child alike, and it moves like a bobsled. It s funny and fun, and if it s not up to Pixar level, it still represents the best of what the competition has to offer.
Puss in Boots doesn t have and doesn t strive for the soul of a Pixar film, but gets pleasure enough out of its own characters and the way they move through this cleverly realized world.

Puss has his charms, but he is not as memorable a character as Shrek or Shrek s mouthy sidekick, Donkey. Consequently the story, which involves a quest for magic beans and golden eggs, feels improvised and diffuse.
A surprisingly delightful adventure romp.

However crass the motivation for its existence, Puss origin story could easily stand on its own -- a testament to clever writing on the part of its creative team and an irresistible central performance by Antonio Banderas.

The seductive interplay of Banderas and Hayek, the barely recognizable vocal contributions of Galifianakis, and the Southern backwoods speech of Thornton and Sedaris all keep us attuned to the events on the screen.

Like most kittens, it s not always perfectly behaved, but at least this new Puss adventure doesn t have you reaching for the cinematic spray bottle. And thank goodness the spin-off does nothing to neuter the charismatic cat s appeal.
Puss made his debut in Shrek 2, then did time in the two decreasingly funny sequels. Now he s got a movie of his own, and not a moment too soon.
